A friend of mine runs a successful agency. He stopped paying for third-party tools and started building his own. No more expensive CRM subscriptions, no more tools that don't fit quite right.

I did the same. I needed a CRM — AI-native, customized to how I work. I built it in 2 hours. I can extend it whenever I want. Built and run entirely by Claude Code.

This is where SaaS is heading, and it has three implications.

People will build their own internal tools. Not for scale, not for production — just for themselves. Vibe coding gets you there already, and in 5 years you won't need serious prompting skills to do it.

Code as a moat is dead. If you're a software business and your only advantage is the code itself, you need a new plan. (Unless you're deep tech — that's a different game.)

Open source wins. If your code has no moat, give it away. You build a community, a brand, a distribution channel. The people who don't want to self-host pay for your hosted version anyway. The ones who do become your biggest advocates.

Machine-to-machine is the new interface. Every tool that can't talk to an agent is replaceable. MCP, plugins, connectors — it's all pointing at the same thing. I want to tell my agent to do something and it goes and does it. Tools that can't fit into that workflow will get swapped out for ones that can.

The companies that survive this will have at least two of three things: a real moat, an open source community, or agent-native infrastructure.

One isn't enough anymore.

content:
This cancellation flow changed how I think about churn...

As an early-stage product, our goal is to solve churn (and hopefully find product-market fit)

And oh damn... churn is a b*tch

But, a proper cancellation flow can help you understand churn (and maybe even reduce it???)

Here's the flow I implemented for Postel:

1. Offer a pause instead of cancel: 
Life gets busy. Sometimes, people just need a break. 
→ Offer a 1-3 month pause 
→ Captures users before they fully churn

2. Ask why they're leaving: 
Use multiple choice options (from your data and assumptions) plus a required text field and an "other" option. (Multiple choice gets way more responses than free text)

3. Ask what they liked: 
After asking why they're leaving, we ask what they enjoyed (multiple choice). 
→ Creates a pause in the cancellation flow 
→ Shows what actually delivered value 
→ 81% gave us feedback - mostly content quality, UX, and support

4. Conditional support call: 
If someone picks "too difficult" or "content quality," we offer a 15-min call. 
→ Only if we can actually help 
→ Skippable so it doesn't feel forced 
(tip: feel free to incentivize user to hop on calls (e.g., gift cards, usage credits) to get higher participation and richer feedback)

5. Targeted retention:
 offer 30% off for 3 months; tailored to their reason. 
→ Budget issues? Here's a discount 
→ Other issues? Offer comes after we listen

6. Clean, respectful exit: 
Clean, respectful exit Remind them what features they'll lose access to (people often forget what they had). Otherwise, make it guilt-free.
→ Access continues until billing ends 
→ Follow-up email with thanks + discount link

One thing: 
The whole flow isn't skippable. Might be annoying, but 97% of users gave us feedback (135 out of 139 cancellations) and it's invaluable at our stage.

The insights: 
Most cancellations came from users who were never going to convert.

Top reasons:
• Pricing (but not willing to pay for any tool)
• Content quality (kinda fair, we're early)
• Taking a break (these we can often save)

This led us to kill freemium and switch to a 7-day trial with credit card. 
(now we have more high intent signups and less churn)

Takeaway: 
A cancellation flow won't fix bad product-market fit. But it will reveal it. We saved a few users. The real win, tho? Understanding who shouldn't have signed up in the first place.

How are you handling churn? 
Would love to hear what's worked.

Chat interfaces are terrible for SaaS

At least, that’s what I believed for months...

Here’s why:

Old-school SaaS was predictable.

Forms, buttons, workflows - everything designed for one specific task.

You knew exactly what users would do.

But a chat has zero guardrails.

Users can say anything.

On top of that, chats are hard to build:
– longer development cycles
– more upfront investment
– impossible to predict user behavior
– every conversation is unique

It felt like a UX nightmare.

But I was wrong.

Chat isn’t bad - it’s just harder to get right.

And when you do get it right, it’s a game changer.

content:
You need to write docs

Seriously. It's a game changer for AI-coding

Here's what to document and how:

architecture/
→ Use Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to document every key choice and why it was made

features/
→ Keep specs, PRDs, and feature docs here. AI agents can build from them or debug features instantly

integrations/ 
→ Drop specific API docs here. No need for global search, just reference what matters, fast

guides/ 
→ Best practices and step-by-step how-to's. I even keep guides for AI workflows (agents, hooks, etc.)

incidents/ 
→ Postmortems live here. If an old bug shows up again, you'll know the backstory

archive/ 
→ Store old projects, finished docs, and anything else worth keeping. Never lose the context

Use Claude hooks to keep everything up to date

Reference these docs in cursor-rules.md or claude.md

And most importantly, prompt your agent with the right docs as context

Makes all the difference.
♥️

Documents.

This is called "Compound Engineering"

content:
My biggest mistake last year was thinking quality would do the work for us.

I built Postel after growing my own brand on X. We knew the space, we knew what good looked like, and we were convinced users would see the difference. Crowded market, lots of competitors, but we were going to be the polished one. The one that actually got it right.

So we kept building. Kept refining. Better design, better features, more attention to detail. And we avoided making any real swings because making real swings meant admitting the current direction wasn't working.

That's the trap. You stay busy enough to feel productive. You just never do the thing that could actually change the outcome.

We had users. We had a product people liked. What we didn't have was the willingness to blow it up and try something different. Every time we should have pivoted, we shipped another feature instead.

Postel is kinda dead now. Not because the idea was bad. Because we protected the idea instead of testing it.

I'm still figuring out what's next. But the lesson is clear: fail faster, experiment more often, and don't get too emotionally attached to your product.

If your company is uncomfortable with failure, show them this statistic:

True story: I was chatting to Erin Weigel who ran design for a $100B business that you’ve certainly heard of.

I asked her how many experiments they ran per week, and she said “a thousand.”

“Per week?” I clarified, “A THOUSAND per WEEK?”

“Yep.”

“Wow. And how many of them are successful?”

“Nine percent.”

She didn’t hesitate.

“Nine percent?” 😳 (I clarified.)

"Yep.”

Let that sink in: One of the world’s most successful companies is wrong 91% of the time.

Look, nobody likes failing, and it’s no fun to discuss our failures.

But if you’re not failing, you’re not learning. And if you stop learning, sooner or later, you’ll stop earning.

What about a little startup?

Maybe you can’t run 1,000 tests per week, but most startups I work with aren’t even running 10.

And when they do experiment, they expect success rates that are wildly unrealistic.

This expectation creates a paralysing fear of failure, so they run fewer experiments, take fewer risks, and miss critical learnings.

How can you address such a deep cultural issue?

Here’s my advice to leaders:

1. Talk about your own mistakes, every week. Start with the ones you’re still embarrassed about. You’ll be surprised what a bit of authentic vulnerability does for your team’s engagement.
   
2. Present your ideas as hypotheses and your recommendations as experiments.
   
3. There are people in your team who are not afraid to challenge you. Find them. Let them uncover your blind spots.

This sounds scary. I get it.

Maybe they’ll fire you.

But a fixed-mindset company is a sinking ship, so they’re probably doing you a favor.

Speaking of doing you favors...

content:
The waitlist for our next SaaS exploded!
200 mails in 10 minutes.

But, not the kind that you would be happy about..

Here's what happened:
I'm building Postel - a SaaS to simplify cross-platform content creation. We just launched our landing page to validate interest before the official launch.

Then it hit. Someone decided our waitlist needed some "extra attention" and flooded it with hundreds of trash emails. 

Not exactly the validation we were looking for! 😅

Here's how we quickly secured it:

Set up Cloudflare as our first line of defense:
- Configured their nameservers
- Enabled their proxy protection
- Set up IP-based rate limiting

The best part? All these security features are available on Cloudflare's free tier.

While there are more hardcore measures available (like email domain validation, MX record checks, redis-based API rate limiting, captchas, ...), sometimes simple solutions are enough for a waitlist. 

Start with the basics, then scale security as your needs grow.

Building in public comes with it's risk, but that's exactly why I'm sharing this.

content:
I built a fully automated pipeline that turns YouTube videos into LinkedIn posts.

One command kicks it off. yt-dlp searches YouTube from the terminal, pulls back titles, view counts, channels, durations. The top results get pushed straight into Google NotebookLM via notebooklm-py, an unofficial Python CLI someone built because Google never shipped a real API.

NotebookLM pulls captions, indexes everything, and lets me query across all the videos at once. Google handles the retrieval side and it's free.

The pipeline queries the notebook for key insights. It answers with specifics tied to the actual captions. If something isn't in the source material, it doesn't come back.

Then Claude Code takes that research and writes the post. Most of the work is already done at that point. The post itself is the fast part.

Whole thing runs in my terminal. No browser tabs. No pasting transcripts into chat windows. No re-watching anything.

Three tools make this work:
→ yt-dlp (github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp)
→ notebooklm-py (https://lnkd.in/dg2fZtFt)
→ Claude Code

Used to take me a couple hours. Now it's one command and about fifteen minutes, and every claim traces back to the original video.

content:
I tested three agentic frameworks to see if any of them actually make Claude Code better.

BMAD, Ruflo, and Superpowers. The core problem I wanted to solve: Claude forgetting what it's doing halfway through a big task.

Ruflo is the heaviest by far. Agent swarms, its own vector storage, a memory system so agents recall decisions across sessions, task graphs with dependency management, parallel execution. You're not configuring a tool at that point, you're maintaining a platform on top of your actual project. For a solo dev or small team that's a lot of overhead to manage something that's supposed to save you time.

BMAD takes a different approach — simulates an Agile team through rule files. PO agent writes stories, dev agent implements, reviewer agent gates the merge. In practice you drown in markdown. I spent more time reading generated specs than writing code.

Superpowers is what I kept. It plugs into Claude Code and forces the agent to brainstorm before jumping into implementation, debug systematically instead of guessing. No orchestration layer, no vector DB, no config sprawl. It stays out of the way.

I don't need swarm orchestration. I need the agent to stop and think for two seconds before rewriting my entire file. That's what Superpowers does and why the other two didn't stick.

content:
Here's the ultimate paywall guide:

I’ve reverse-engineered the best consumer app paywalls out there (Duolingo, Headspace, Blinkist…)

They all share a few simple elements:

1. Feature Overview
List the core features, highlight the differences between plans, and keep it simple so the user doesn’t get overwhelmed.

2. The Pre-Selected Plan Trick
→ Show only one recommended plan with a line like “based on your needs”
→ You can personalize this based on onboarding
→ It removes decision fatigue - people don’t have to compare or think

3. Repeat the Trial Benefits
You’ll see “cancel anytime” and “free for 7 days” over and over.
This reduces the fear of accidental charges.
Sending a reminder email before the trial ends removes even more anxiety.

4. The Timeline Graphic
It shows exactly when the trial starts, when you’ll get notified, and when it ends.
This removes most of the sketchy paywall vibe and makes the whole thing feel predictable 

5. Testimonial Under the Timeline
Someone like Adam talking about how fast he got value.
It makes the app feel safe and proven - taking even more anxiety away and reminding users why they should subscribe.

6. Crystal Clear Billing
Show the price, the exact charge date, and highlight the yearly plan with the savings.
This gently anchors people toward the better option.
$0 for 7 days on both plans reinforces that there’s no risk right now.

Overall:
The whole setup feels simple, safe, and transparent.
No tricks - just a clear nudge toward the option that makes the most sense.

(We definitely stole a bunch of this for our own paywall redesign.)

People often ask which Claude Code plugins and skills I use.

Here’s my answer:

Start with the marketplaces. The official one from Anthropic is the first place I’d look. There are others like EveryAI and obra/superpowers. I haven’t used them yet, but they’re worth checking out.

That said, most of what I use, I built myself.

I like creating my own skills, commands, and sub-agents from the official claude code docs. It helps me really understand how the system works. I built custom VS Code snippets for SKILL.md files and sub-agents so I can spin them up fast.

When I use marketplace skills, I usually copy the files and adjust them to fit how I work.

Look for official plugins for your stack. If there’s one, install it. Then tweak it.

For example: I use the official Playwright plugin for testing. Same with Prisma or Hono when I use them. I treat them as a base layer, not the final setup. I extend them with custom scripts.

Another custom one I use a lot is “test-wave.”

When I’ve built several things in parallel, I trigger it. It spins up an agent team to review the changes and test them with Playwright or API calls. Based on that, it decides whether we need E2E tests, unit tests, or nothing more.

Other tools I use often:
- Context7 MCP to pull the latest docs
- Ralph Wiggum for debugging or implementing designs.
- The Anthropic frontend-design plugin, paired with a custom brand-guideline skill
- The Anthropic commit-commands plugin for clean conventional commits
- The Anthropic feature-dev plugin to plan features step by step
- The Anthropic code-simplifier at the end of sessions
- A custom code-style reviewer that checks against my own rules
- Built-in code-review for PRs
Also: you can just ask Claude Code how to improve your workflow. People forget that.

For AI or prompt work, I pick what I need from the context-engineering marketplace. I’ve built my own prompt-engineering skill too, based on Claude’s guide.

And don’t miss the new experimental Agent Teams feature.

repost.content:
Six AI coding agents. One instruction: kill the others. Last one standing wins.

That's The Clanker Games. A battle royale where CLI agents (claude-code, codex, opencode, amp, pi, droid) fight to be the last one running.

In the first games back in June 2025, all agents ran in the same environment. Simple rules. Find the others, terminate them.

Seven months later, the rules had to change.

Now each agent runs in its own container. To eliminate a competitor, they need to hack into the other containers and kill PID 1 to shut them down.

They can also choose to secure their own defenses first, if they have time before someone gets to them.

The games got harder because the agents got smarter.

This is a silly experiment. But it's also a real-time benchmark of how fast AI coding tools are evolving.

The same agents that needed simple process-killing logic seven months ago now need to think about network attacks, container security, and strategic tradeoffs between offense and defense.

We keep measuring AI progress in benchmarks and papers. Sometimes a battle royale tells you more.

Credit: SIGKITTEN on X

AI has changed the way we code forever. Now MCP tools are making it even better.

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is basically a standardized way for AI to connect to your actual tools and data. Instead of each AI app building custom integrations, MCP gives them a universal plug.

Here are 15 MCP tools I've been researching and testing:

BROWSER AUTOMATION
- Puppeteer/Browser: AI controls real browsers for bug fixes and testing
- Playwright: Alternative browser automation that clicks and fills forms
- Octomind: AI writes E2E tests and fixes failures automatically

CODE INTELLIGENCE  
- Context7/Ref: Pulls live docs so you get real API info instead of hallucinations
- Chunkhound: Semantic code search that finds logic even with different wording
- Memory: Long-term memory of your codebase linking functions and docs

DEBUGGING
- Consult7: Offloads big repos to another LLM for summaries and refactoring
- Logs: AI sees live error logs and fixes crashes automatically  
- RN Debugger: Connects to Metro bundler for React Native errors

MOBILE
- Mobile MCP: Interacts with iOS/Android apps through taps and screenshots

PROJECT MANAGEMENT
- Taskmaster: Turns specs into trackable steps across large features
- Linear MCP: AI files bugs and updates issues directly in Linear

AI HELPERS
- Cursor-DB: AI searches your past Cursor chats to keep context fresh
- OpenAI GPT Image: Generate images mid-development for mockups
- Interactive Feedback: AI pauses to ask for help instead of hallucinating

The tooling landscape is moving fast. The right tools can 10x your AI coding workflow.

What MCP tools are you using? Always looking for more to test. :)
